title: A MAN AND HIS FATHER WERE GOING TO THE SAME WOMAN—And Amos Named It as Part of Israel’s Corruption
paragraphs: A MAN AND HIS FATHER WERE GOING TO THE SAME WOMAN—And Amos Named It as Part of Israel’s Corruption

Amos 2:7 exposes something darker than sexual scandal. It shows what happens when people still approach the things of God while compassion, purity, justice, and reverence are quietly dying inside them.
There are verses in the Bible we read slowly because they comfort us.
And then there are verses we almost wish we had misread.
Amos 2:7 is one of them.
The prophet is confronting Israel when, without softening the words or protecting anyone's reputation, he says:
וְאִישׁ וְאָבִיו יֵלְכוּ אֶל־הַנַּעֲרָה לְמַעַן חַלֵּל אֶת־שֵׁם קָדְשִׁי
Ve’ish ve’aviv yelkhu el-hanna‘arah, lema‘an challel et-shem qodshi.
Literally, the Hebrew says that “a man and his father go to the young woman” and that through this God’s holy name is profaned.
Read that again.
A man.
His father.
The young woman.
And God says:
My holy name is being profaned.
The scandal is real. But if all we see is sexual scandal, we may miss the terrifying reason Amos put this sentence where he did.
Because Amos did not suddenly interrupt an otherwise peaceful sermon to give Israel some juicy story about somebody's bedroom.
Look at what surrounds the verse.

People were being sold over debts. The needy were being treated as though their lives were worth little more than a pair of sandals. The poor were being crushed. The vulnerable were being pushed aside. Then comes the man and his father going to the young woman. Immediately afterward, Amos describes people reclining beside altars on garments taken in pledge and drinking wine obtained through imposed fines.
Money.
Power.
Sex.
The vulnerable.
Religion.
All tangled together.
That is the nightmare Amos is exposing.
Israel had reached a place where people could exploit human beings and still get close enough to an altar to pretend everything between them and God was fine.
And maybe that is why this ancient passage is more uncomfortable than we want it to be.
Because corruption rarely begins when somebody wakes up and decides, “Today I will become evil.”
It begins smaller.
One compromise.
One excuse.
One appetite nobody confronts.
One person treated as an object.
One secret protected because exposure would be embarrassing.
One injustice ignored because confronting it would cost something.
One sin renamed because repentance feels too painful.
And eventually a person can become so accustomed to darkness that what once would have broken his heart becomes normal.
That is one of sin's most frightening abilities.
It does not merely tempt you to do something wrong.
If repeatedly embraced and defended, it can train you to stop being shocked by what is wrong.
The Hebrew makes Amos's accusation especially sobering.

The woman is called הַנַּעֲרָה — hanna‘arah, meaning “the young woman” or “the girl.” Scripture does not explicitly tell us her precise identity here. Some interpreters understand the passage as sexual exploitation of a vulnerable or servant woman; others have connected it with a cultic setting because verse 8 immediately mentions the altar. Many translations understand the statement sexually. But responsible reading should not pretend the Hebrew tells us more than it actually does.

The Hebrew expression itself is literally that the man and his father “go to” the young woman. Most interpreters have understood sexual immorality to be involved, though scholars have debated the precise situation because the usual Hebrew expression for sexual relations is different.
That uncertainty matters.
Not because it makes Amos less serious.
It makes us listen more carefully.
We do not need to invent details to make God's Word shocking.
The words God actually gave us are enough.
And the conclusion Amos gives us is unmistakable:
לְמַעַן חַלֵּל אֶת־שֵׁם קָדְשִׁי
“…to profane My holy name.”
That is where the knife turns.
Their sin was not merely damaging themselves.
They were dragging God's holy name through the consequences of their behavior.
They belonged to the covenant people.
They carried His name.
They worshiped.
They approached altars.
And their lives were telling lies about the God they claimed to know.
That should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Because Christianity is not merely saying the right things about Jesus.
You can know worship songs and still hide corruption.
You can quote Scripture and still mistreat people.
You can post Bible verses while secretly feeding an appetite that is destroying your soul.
You can appear spiritual publicly while becoming spiritually numb privately.
You can defend biblical morality online while refusing to repent of what happens when nobody is watching.
Amos will not allow us to separate worship from character.
He will not allow us to praise God with our mouths while trampling people made in God's image with our lives.
And Jesus will not allow that separation either.

Christ's strongest confrontations were often directed not merely toward visibly broken sinners, but toward religious hypocrisy—the terrifying condition in which somebody learns how to look clean without becoming clean.
That is why this story is not ultimately about pointing at ancient Israel and whispering:
“How disgusting.”
It is about standing before the Word of God and asking:
Lord… where have I become comfortable with what once convicted me?
That question is harder.
Where have you started calling compromise “normal”?
What have you hidden behind a locked screen?
Whose dignity have you ignored because satisfying yourself mattered more?
What relationship are you keeping that continually pulls you away from Christ?
What secret would terrify you if everyone at church knew?
What bitterness have you baptized as “discernment”?
What greed have you renamed “ambition”?
What lust have you renamed “a struggle” while refusing to cut off the things continually feeding it?
What injustice have you ignored because speaking would inconvenience you?
What have you been asking God to forgive while quietly arranging to do it again?
Those questions hurt.
But conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because if Amos 2 were the end of the biblical story, all we would have is exposure.
Sin uncovered.
Hypocrisy exposed.
Judgment approaching.
No escape.
But Amos is not the end of the story.
Jesus Christ entered it.
The holy God whose name humanity has profaned did something sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
The Son of God came near.
Not to approve our corruption.
Not to rename our sin.
Not to pretend holiness no longer matters.
He came to save sinners from it.
Jesus touched people respectable religion avoided.
He defended the vulnerable.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He welcomed the ashamed.
He forgave the guilty who came to Him.
And then He went to a cross carrying something He never personally possessed:
our guilt.
Think about the contrast.
Amos shows human beings profaning God's holy name through sin.
At Calvary, Jesus bears shame to rescue the very people who have dishonored that name.
He was mocked.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
And the scandal of human sin collided with the grace of God.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that shrugs at evil.
Grace purchased through blood.
Grace that forgives and then begins transforming.
Grace that does not say, “Your sin never mattered.”
Grace says:
Your sin mattered so much that Christ died—and His mercy is so great that your sin does not have to own you anymore.
That changes everything.
Maybe your scandal does not look like Amos 2:7.
Maybe nobody knows yours.
Maybe your scandal lives in browser history.
Maybe it lives inside resentment.
Maybe it happened years ago and still whispers your name at night.
Maybe somebody used you, and you have spent years carrying shame that belonged to the person who sinned against you.
Maybe you were the betrayer.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Maybe someone destroyed yours.
Maybe you have walked into church smiling while privately wondering whether God could possibly want somebody who has done what you have done.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend the past was beautiful.
The Gospel announces that Jesus is powerful enough to redeem what sin has shattered.
Repentance does not mean hiding.
Repentance means turning.
Turning from sin.
Turning toward Christ.
Bringing into His light what darkness told you must remain hidden forever.
There is a reason 1 John tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not excuse.
Cleanse.
There is a reason Paul could speak of people whose former lives were marked by devastating sins and then say:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That word carries resurrection inside it.
You were not created to spend the rest of your life chained to the worst chapter you ever wrote.
Jesus Christ does not merely edit sinners.
He makes people new.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing Christianity means becoming skilled at concealing the evidence.
It doesn't.
The cross means you can finally stop hiding.
Bring the pornography into the light.
Bring the affair into the light.
Bring the dishonesty into the light.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the greed.
Bring the secret messages.
Bring the double life.
Bring the wound.
Bring the shame.
Bring the thing you cannot type publicly.
Bring it to Jesus.

And where your sin has harmed another person, repentance may also require truth, accountability, restitution, changed boundaries, and accepting consequences rather than merely asking God to make the discomfort disappear.
Grace is free.
Repentance is not fake.
Transformation has fruit.
That is why Amos still matters.
God cares about what happens to vulnerable people.
God cares about sexual integrity.
God cares about justice.
God cares about how money is obtained.
God cares about what happens outside the worship service.
God cares about what His people do with power.
God cares about His holy name.
And if we claim the name of Jesus, our private lives are not spiritually irrelevant.
But neither is our failure beyond His reach.
Peter denied Christ and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians and became a servant of Christ.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history and encountered the Messiah.
The woman caught in adultery encountered neither permission to continue in sin nor permission for self-righteous men to destroy her.
Again and again, Jesus enters stories human beings would rather throw away.
And He rewrites them.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It means sin does not get the final word.
Your past does not get the final word.
Your addiction does not get the final word.
Your abuser does not get the final word.
Your failure does not get the final word.
Your shame does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
So perhaps the most important response to Amos 2:7 is not:
“Look how corrupt those people were.”
Perhaps it is:
“Jesus, search me.”
Talk to God.
Tell the truth.
Repent.
Seek wise pastoral or Christian accountability where needed.
If another person's abuse or exploitation is involved, bringing darkness into the light does not mean placing yourself back into danger; seek safe, trustworthy help.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes a small public confession becomes the moment somebody finally stops pretending.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, do not hide the testimony forever.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Somebody reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches ruined places.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because somebody you know may be smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
Send it privately to the person God puts on your heart.
There may come a night when temptation starts negotiating again.
There may come a morning when shame starts preaching again.
Come back and remember:
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become comfortable in chains.
He came to set captives free.
It cannot.
The Gospel is grace.
But Gospel ministry requires people willing to participate in carrying truth farther.

We should be careful with the word tithe. Give first as Scripture and conscience direct you, support your local church and faithful ministry, care for people in need, and never confuse financial support with salvation.
But if you have been asking, “How can I help this ministry continue?”
This is one tangible way.
Your support can help us keep writing.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep placing Scripture in front of people who may never walk through a church door before they encounter truth on a screen.
And comment.
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Maybe Amos exposed something.
Maybe Jesus is calling something out of hiding.
Maybe today is finally the day you stop protecting the thing that has been destroying you.
Because the most frightening part of Amos 2:7 is not that Israel became scandalous.
It is that people could become comfortable with corruption while remaining close to religious things.
And the most beautiful part of the Gospel is that Jesus still walks directly into the wreckage and calls sinners home.
So come home.
Not when you have cleaned yourself enough.
Not when your history becomes less embarrassing.
Not after you manufacture a respectable testimony.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Let Him expose what needs exposing.
Forgive what He commands you to forgive.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repair what can rightly be repaired.
Leave what needs leaving.
Seek help where you need help.
And follow Jesus.
Because there is something greater than having a spotless history.
There is having a Redeemer.
The scandal may explain how you arrived here. It does not have the authority to decide where Jesus will take you next.
